title: Singing it for someone
hookLine: a shabad sung for a sick or grieving friend is a gift
last: THE FOREST AT HOME · ALL MUST GO · ACCEPTED · OUR SHABAD · THE RIGHT SONG · BY HEART.

lines: FLOWERS WILT, WORDS COME OUT WRONG.
cards: What do you say to a friend whose father just died? What do you bring to a hospital room? Flowers wilt, food piles up, and words come out wrong.
Even a kind text can feel thin. Some Sikh families have an old answer. They sit by the bed, or in the living room of the grieving house, and they sing.
Not performers: aunties, cousins, a neighbor with a harmonium. Today: singing it for someone.

teach.h: A GIFT GIVEN WITH YOUR VOICE.
teach.b: In Sikh life, a shabad can be a gift you give with your voice.
When someone is ill, families often gather for a reading of Sukhmani Sahib, the Psalm of Peace, or for kirtan at home, and end with an Ardas asking for the person's wellbeing.

When someone has died, the sangat gathers at the family's house in the days that follow, for readings and kirtan, so the family isn't alone with the silence. What gets sung? Often a shabad of comfort.
One line turned to in illness comes from Sukhmani Sahib, on Ang two seventy-four.
In paraphrase: the Name is the medicine for every illness. Others sing the hot wind that doesn't touch, or the Name that destroys pain. Why singing, and not just talking?
Sikhs give a few reasons. The words aren't yours: you don't have to find the perfect thing to say, because the Guru has already said it.
Singing is shared: the sick person can listen with their eyes closed, and nobody has to make conversation. And it carries something beyond the singer.
Sikhs understand the shabad as the Guru's own voice, so singing it for someone offers them the Guru's company, not just yours.

teach.h: IT DOESN'T HAVE TO BE GOOD.
teach.b: The quiet part: it doesn't have to be good.
A wobbly voice, a phone playing a recording, a line whispered at a bedside. The gift is the attention, and the Word.

how: When someone is ill or has died, Sikh families and friends often gather at home for Sukhmani Sahib, kirtan and Ardas, singing shabads of comfort for the person and the family.

practice: Think of someone who's sick, tired or grieving right now, and picture their face. Take your two lines from yesterday, or any line you love, and say or hum them softly, as if for that person, without worrying how it sounds.
If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them.

wordCard.voice: Aukhad, medicine: a shabad given to a sick or grieving friend is medicine too, the Guru's words offered with your own voice, however it sounds.
